# 1.1 - Integers & Number Lines {.unnumbered}

Did you know that all of mathematics is actually built up from simple things like counting? Even advanced topics like {{< glink algebra >}} and {{< glink calculus >}} are just clever ways of organizing and extending basic ideas (like moving forward and backward on a {{< glink "number line" >}}).

In this lesson, we’ll use the number line not just to count, but to add, subtract, and compare {{< glink positive >}} and {{< glink negative >}} numbers. That might sound basic, but it’s the foundation of nearly everything else you’ll do in Algebra.

Negative numbers can be confusing, especially when the rules do not match what you expect. But if you can master the way they work on the number line (including things like {{< glink slug="opposite" text="opposites" >}}, {{< glink "absolute value" >}}, and comparison) you’ll be setting yourself up for success in the rest of the course.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I know how to read and use a number line
- [ ] I can find and describe the opposite of a number
- [ ] I can find the absolute value of an integer on a number line
- [ ] I can compare positive and negative numbers using >, <, and =
- [ ] I can add and subtract integers on a number line
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 1.1.1 - The Number Line Is More Than Just Counting

You already know how to count (0, 1, 2, 3, and so on). The **number line** extends that idea in both directions.


**Let’s draw a number line from -10 to 10**
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/blank_numberline.png)

Here, every tick mark is an {{< glink integer >}} (a whole number).

- Numbers to the **right** of zero are {{< glink positive >}}
- Numbers to the **left** of zero are {{< glink negative >}}

We can use this number line to *see* what happens when we add, subtract, or compare numbers.

**Are there other ways to draw a number line?**

Yes! Number lines can be drawn over different ranges and scales. For example, here is a number line that counts from -10 to 25 in steps of 5.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/count_by_5s.png)

In fact, number lines don't even have to be {{< glink horizontal >}}. Here is a {{< glink vertical >}} number line that goes from 0 to 100 in steps of 10.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/vertical_by_tens.png)

:::{.gotcha title="How many numbers are between any two numbers on the number line?"}

**Example 1:** How many numbers between 3 and 5?

If you are counting integers, there is 1 {{< glink integer >}} between 3 and 5 (just 4). But if you mean {{< glink slug="real-number" text="real numbers" >}}, there are {{< glink infinitely >}} many between 3 and 5. Here are some number lines that might help convince you.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/three_to_five_by_1.png)
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/between_3_and_5_by_05.png)
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/between_3_and_5_by_025.png)
:::

:::{.think title="Can you think of any real world examples of number lines?"}

Here are a few examples:

- thermometer
- ruler
- timeline
- American football field
- volume slider on a phone 
:::



***

### 1.1.2 - Understanding Opposites

Let’s look at a pair of numbers, 3 and -3.

These are called {{< glink opposite >}} numbers. They are the **same distance** from zero but on **opposite sides** of it.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/opposites.png)

:::{.think title="What is the opposite of zero?"}

The opposite of zero is zero. Zero is the only number that is its own opposite!
:::

***

### 1.1.3 - What Is Absolute Value?

{{< glink "Absolute value" >}} measures the **distance from zero**. Absolute value is written as a number between two bars. For example, **the absolute value of -5** is written $|-5|$.


Take a look at the number -5. The number line shows that its absolute value is 5 because it is 5 units away from zero.
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/absolute_value_negative_five.png)


You can see that |5| is also 5 for the same reason!
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/absolute_value_five.png)

:::{.real-world}
Absolute value is often used for describing the distance between two points. Suppose you live 3 miles to the east of the school and your best friend lives 5 miles to the west. How far apart are your houses? This is easy to see with a number line.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/east_to_west.png)

You can compute your distances by adding |-5| + |3|, by |-5 - 3|, or by |3 - (-5)|. All three of these give the same answer, 8 miles. What would change if we did not use absolute value?
:::

:::{.think title="Can the absolute value ever be negative?"}

Absolute value is **never** negative, because distance is never negative.
:::

### 1.1.4 - Comparing Integers

There is only one rule, and the number line gives it to you: **whichever number sits farther to the right is the greater one.**

Compare 2 to -7.
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/order_2_and_neg7.png)

2 is to the right of -7, so 2 is {{< glink "greater than" >}} -7. We write that $2 > -7$, or the same thing the other way round, $-7 < 2$.

**Two negatives take a second look.** Compare -4 to -5.
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/order_neg4_and_neg5.png)

-4 is to the right of -5, so $-4 > -5$ - even though 5 sounds like the bigger number. Going left to right, the negatives count *up*: $-5 < -4 < -3$.

:::{.gotcha title="Which is bigger?"}
Two questions sound alike but are not:

- **Which is greater?** asks which number is farther to the **right**.
- **Which has the greater absolute value?** asks which number is farther **from zero**.

They can disagree. Here $-7 < 2$, but $|-7| > |2|$:

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/compare_2_to_neg7.png)
:::

***

### 1.1.5 - Adding and Subtracting Negatives

Money is the easiest way to think about a negative number. A positive number is
money you **have**. A negative number is money you **owe**.

* $+6$ - six dollars in your pocket
* $-6$ - a six dollar debt

Adding is what happens when something is **given** to you. Subtracting is what
happens when something is **taken away**.

***

**Adding**

Adding a positive makes you richer. Adding a negative - a debt - makes you poorer.

$$
-2 + 6 = 4
$$

You are $\$2$ in debt. Someone pays you $\$6$. The debt is cleared and you have
$\$4$ left over.

![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_1/add_6_to_neg2.png)

On the number line, adding $6$ moves you six steps to the right, from $-2$ to $4$.

***

**Subtracting**

Here is the move that makes all of this easier:

:::{.remember}
**Subtracting is the same as adding the opposite.**

$$
a - b = a + (-b)
$$
:::

You met {{< glink "opposite" >}}s back in 1.1.2. This is where opposites become useful.
Instead of two operations with four separate rules to remember, there is only
**one** operation - addition. Every subtraction gets rewritten first.

$$
400 - 450 = 400 + (-450) = -50
$$

You had $\$400$ and spent $\$450$. You are $\$50$ overdrawn.

***

**Subtracting a negative**

This is the one that feels strange, and the money story settles it.

$$
201 - (-5) = 201 + 5 = 206
$$

You had $\$201$. The bank had charged you a $\$5$ fee - a $-5$ sitting in
your account. Then they admitted the mistake and **took the fee away**.

Taking away a debt leaves you better off. That is the whole reason subtracting a
negative makes the answer **bigger**.

:::{.gotcha title="Two signs in a row"}
When two signs end up next to each other, rewrite **before** you compute.

* $7 - (-3)$ becomes $7 + 3 = 10$
* $7 + (-3)$ becomes $7 - 3 = 4$

Rewriting first is what keeps these two apart. Do not try to do it in your head.
:::

***

**More examples**

Rewrite each as an addition, then find the value.

| | Rewrite | Value | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| $5 - 8$ | $5 + (-8)$ | $-3$ | had $\$5$, spent $\$8$, now $\$3$ overdrawn |
| $-4 - 3$ | $-4 + (-3)$ | $-7$ | owed $\$4$, borrowed $\$3$ more |
| $-6 - (-10)$ | $-6 + 10$ | $4$ | owed $\$6$, a $\$10$ debt was cancelled |
| $-9 + 4$ | already an addition | $-5$ | owed $\$9$, paid back $\$4$ |

:::{.think title="Why does the number line stop helping here?"}

For $-2 + 6$ you can count six steps and see the answer appear. For
$201 - (-5)$ there is nothing to count - you would have to know the answer
before you could draw the picture. The number line is good for showing you
**what a negative number is**; the money story is what explains **what happens
when you add and subtract them**.
:::
